intro.text: Ultrasound (US) guided arthrocentesis has become an increasingly valuable tool in the emergency department (ED) for evaluating acute monoarticular arthopathies, particularly septic arthritis, which occurs at an annual rate of 10 per 100,000 patients in the United States.

intro.text: Blockade of the suprascapular nerve is an effective method for providing anesthesia and analgesia for the shoulder.

intro.text: The suprascapular nerve contributes to the sensory innervation of the acromioclavicular and glenohumeral joints and provides motor innervation to the supraspinatus and infraspinatus muscles.

anatomy.text: The suprascapular nerve comprises motor and sensory fibers arising from the C5 and C6 spinal nerves; occasionally, fibers from C4 also contribute.

anatomy.text: The fibers that form the suprascapular nerve are initially contained within the upper trunk of the brachial plexus, but the nerve branches from the upper trunk in the neck and courses laterally, parallel to the inferior belly of the omohyoid muscle, toward the superior border of the scapula.

indications.text: A suprascapular nerve block can be used to treat chronic, acute, and perioperative shoulder pain.

intro.text: Piriformis muscle injection represents an image-guided interventional approach used in the diagnosis and management of sciatic nerve–related pain originating from the deep gluteal region.
intro.title: Piriformis Injection

intro.text: Clinical application targets patients with suspected piriformis-related sciatic irritation, particularly when conservative therapy fails or diagnostic uncertainty persists.
intro.title: Piriformis Injection

anatomy.text: A piriformis muscle injection requires a precise understanding of regional anatomy, pain-generating physiology, and the mechanisms of sciatic nerve irritation within the deep gluteal space (see Image.
anatomy.title: Piriformis Injection

anatomy.text: Symptom generation in piriformis-related sciatic pain reflects entrapment and subsequent irritation of the sciatic nerve by a spastic piriformis muscle, a process analogous to myofascial pain syndromes.
anatomy.title: Piriformis Injection

indications.text: Piriformis muscle injection is considered in patients with persistent sciatic-type pain originating from the deep gluteal region, particularly when conservative therapy fails, symptoms recur despite pharmacologic management, or diagnostic uncertainty persists after exclusion of alternative etiologies.
indications.title: Piriformis Injection

indications.text: Clinical presentations prompting consideration of injection may occur acutely in posttraumatic cases or more insidiously in the setting of overuse or myofascial pain mechanisms.
indications.title: Piriformis Injection

indications.text: Patients commonly report gluteal pain accompanied by paresthesias affecting the back, groin, perineum, upper gluteal region, hip, posterior thigh, calf, foot, or rectum.
indications.title: Piriformis Injection

contra.text: Absolute contraindications to piriformis injection include patient refusal, local or systemic infection, and clinically significant coagulopathy or anticoagulation that cannot be safely managed peri-procedurally.
contra.title: Piriformis Injection

contra.text: Known hypersensitivity to the planned injectate, contrast agent, or other procedural medications is also a contraindication.
contra.title: Piriformis Injection

contra.text: Relative contraindications include inability to cooperate with positioning or procedural instructions, distorted regional anatomy that limits safe needle placement, and uncontrolled medical comorbidities that may increase procedural risk.
contra.title: Piriformis Injection

technique.text: After a local anesthetic is used for skin and subcutaneous anesthesia, a longer spinal or Quincke needle is advanced toward the piriformis muscle.
technique.title: Piriformis Injection

technique.title: Piriformis Injection

technique.title: Piriformis Injection

complications.text: Complications of piriformis injection are uncommon but may include bleeding, infection, postinjection soreness, transient worsening of pain, headache, allergic or other adverse reactions to the injectate, and failure of the procedure to provide meaningful symptom relief.
complications.title: Piriformis Injection

complications.text: Because of the proximity of the sciatic nerve and surrounding gluteal neurovascular structures, inadvertent nerve irritation or injury remains an important procedural risk, particularly when needle localization is inaccurate.
complications.title: Piriformis Injection

complications.title: Piriformis Injection

significance.text: Piriformis injection holds significant clinical value as both a diagnostic and therapeutic intervention for patients with refractory upper gluteal and sciatic-type leg pain originating from deep gluteal pathology.

intro.text: Sacroiliac joint (SIJ) pain is a common contributor to mechanical low back pain, accounting for approximately 10% to 27% of cases.

anatomy.title: Sacroiliac Joint Injection

intro.text: Facet joint injections are one of the most commonly performed procedures amongst all spinal interventions.
intro.title: Facet Joint Injection

intro.text: Facet joint pain can arise from osteoarthritis, segmental instability, trauma, meniscoid impingement, and inflammatory synovitis.
intro.title: Facet Joint Injection

anatomy.text: The facet joint (zygapophyseal joints) are located throughout the spine and vary in size and shape depending on the vertebral level.
anatomy.title: Facet Joint Injection

anatomy.text: They are synovial joints formed by the articular processes between two adjacent vertebrae.
anatomy.title: Facet Joint Injection

indications.text: Prior to facet joint injections, it is recommended that conservative treatments are trialed for at least 3 months, including multimodal medication management, physical therapy, and behavioral modifications.
indications.title: Facet Joint Injection

indications.text: It is also important to note the presence of moderate to severe pain burden with pain scores > 4/10 on the numeric pain scale, as well as an associated compromise in functionality or quality of life.
indications.title: Facet Joint Injection

indications.text: Indications for therapeutic facet joint injection include patients with confirmed facet joint pain who responded to diagnostic facet joint injection, adjunct to conservative pain management, in patients who are unable to manage pain with oral or systemic drug therapy, pain due to adjacent segment deterioration after spinal fusion, pain due to spondylolytic defects.
indications.title: Facet Joint Injection

contra.text: There are no absolute contraindications besides patient refusal.
contra.title: Facet Joint Injection

contra.text: Relative contraindications include patients with systemic or local infection over the injection site, coagulopathy or bleeding diathesis (particularly with the cervical region), allergy to contrast agent or medications, a neurologic disorder that may be masked by procedure, and pregnancy.

complications.title: Facet Joint Injection

significance.text: Although pain stemming from facet joint etiology is common, the diagnosis is challenging due to non-specific findings on physical exam, history, and imaging that may overlap with other pain pathologies.

intro.text: Myofascial trigger points are focal "knots" located in a taut band of skeletal muscle first described by Dr.

intro.text: These points are usually palpable and produce a characteristic referred pain upon palpation, along with pain locally and occasionally a local twitch response.

anatomy.text: Pathogenesis of trigger points is thought to be related to abnormal motor end-plates within a muscle where the motor and nociceptive nerves co-exist, with a component of enhanced central sensitization in the spinal cord.

indications.text: These factors assist in breaking the pain-tension cycle.

intro.text: Elbow arthrocentesis is a procedure performed to aspirate the contents of a joint cavity to evaluate and treat elbow effusion.

anatomy.text: The distal humerus, radial head, and olecranon comprise the elbow joint.
anatomy.title: Elbow Arthrocentesis

anatomy.title: Elbow Arthrocentesis

indications.title: Elbow Arthrocentesis

indications.text: Diagnostically, the primary etiologies of concern are septic arthritis, hemarthrosis, and inflammation.

contra.title: Elbow Arthrocentesis

dexa.text: Osteopenia, or low bone mass, refers to a reduction in bone mineral density (BMD) below normal reference values without fulfilling the diagnostic criteria for osteoporosis.
dexa.title: Osteopenia

dexa.text: BMD is measured using dual-energy x-ray absorptiometry (DXA).
dexa.title: Osteopenia

dexa.text: According to the World Health Organization (WHO), osteopenia is defined by a T-score between -1.0 and -2.5, while a T-score less than -2.5 indicates osteoporosis.
dexa.title: Osteopenia

dexa.text: In individuals without identifiable risk factors, most clinicians recommend screening with DXA in women approaching menopause or age 65, and in men at age 70.

dexa.text: Osteoporosis (translating to 'porous bones' from the Greek words Osteon and Poros) is characterized by low bone mineral density (BMD) with a propensity for fractures.
dexa.title: Osteoporosis in Females

dexa.text: The average decrease in BMD over the menopausal transition is between 10% and 12% in the spine and hip (1 T-score unit), meaning half of the women are losing bone even faster, with up to 20% loss in the 7 years around menopause.
dexa.title: Osteoporosis in Females

dexa.text: In 1994, the WHO provided a radiological definition of osteoporosis, with a BMD of -2.5 standard deviations (SD) or lower than the mean value for young adult women (T-score of ≤ - 2.5 SD) on dual-energy x-ray absorptiometry (DEXA) of the lumbar spine, femoral neck, total proximal femur or distal one-third (33%) of the radius.
dexa.title: Osteoporosis in Females

dexa.text: The WHO provides a further category, known as ‘severe’ (established) osteoporosis, which includes a T-score of ≤-2.5 SD and 1 or more fragility fractures.
dexa.title: Osteoporosis in Females

dexa.text: While a T-score of ≤-2.5 SD confers the greatest risk for fracture, overall, there are more fractures with a T-score of –1.0 to –2.5 SD due to more patients in this category.
dexa.title: Osteoporosis in Females

dexa.text: Therefore, osteoporosis can be diagnosed with a T-score between -1.0 and -2.5 SD if there is an increased fracture risk using risk-assessment tools (with country-specific thresholds).
dexa.title: Osteoporosis in Females

dexa.text: Conditions Associated With Osteoporosis) Uniquely, diabetes has recently been demonstrated as an osteoporosis and subsequent fracture risk factor despite a relatively normal or even elevated bone mineral density (BMD).
dexa.title: Osteoporosis in Males

dexa.text: The Endocrine Society recommends performing a dual-energy x-ray absorptiometry (DEXA) scan of the spine and hip in men at risk for osteoporosis, and the forearm DEXA scan (a one-third portion of the dominant radius) is recommended when the lumbar spine or hip BMD cannot be reliably interpreted as well as for men with hyperparathyroidism or on androgen deprivation therapy.
dexa.title: Osteoporosis in Males

dexa.text: A diagnosis of osteoporosis in men older than 50 years of age can be made with a history of a fragility fracture or in those whose BMD T-score is ≤-2.5 standard deviations (SD).
dexa.title: Osteoporosis in Males

dexa.text: Both the ISCD and WHO endorse a young female reference database to calculate T-scores in men; however, clinicians should be aware that many institutions may use a sex-specific reference database.
dexa.title: Osteoporosis in Males

dexa.text: The latter approach of using sex-specific database ranges is preferred, as many trials assessing treatment in males with osteoporosis used T-scores calculated using normal male controls.
dexa.title: Osteoporosis in Males

dexa.text: In men younger than 50, BMD is insufficient for diagnosis of osteoporosis, and a diagnosis requires a Z-score of ≤-2.0 SD in addition to a major risk factor or history of fragility fracture.
dexa.title: Osteoporosis in Males

dexa.text: Z-scores instead of T-scores should be used in bone density evaluation for this age bracket.
dexa.title: Secondary Osteoporosis

dexa.text: The National Osteoporosis Foundation recommends using a T-score of less than -2.5 for the diagnosis of osteoporosis in both men and women and a Z-score of -2.0 or lower for a younger age.
dexa.title: Secondary Osteoporosis

dexa.text: All patients awaiting transplants should have a baseline DXA scan.
dexa.title: Secondary Osteoporosis

dexa.text: Patients should have a baseline DXA for evaluation of bone health.
dexa.title: Secondary Osteoporosis

dexa.text: Guidelines suggest screening for low BMD with DXA from age 18 years old and above in all patients with cystic fibrosis or earlier if the patients have increased risk factors for further bone loss.
dexa.title: Secondary Osteoporosis

dexa.text: In the physical exam, there may also be thoracic kyphosis and loss of height from vertebral compression fractures, but more frequently, osteoporosis is initially completely asymptomatic, and it is usually detected either by a DXA scan or by a fragility fracture.
